questions.title: Why does preserving hyperspherical energy help maintain semantic fidelity in diffusion models?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that keeping the hyperspherical energy of a layer unchanged preserves the semantic generation ability. Intuitively, mine: hyperspherical energy reflects pairwise cosine similarities among neurons. But how does this metric directly correlate with the downstream image semantics? Are there theoretical or empirical results showing that large deviations in this metric lead to loss of subject identity or controllability? What would happen if we only minimized Euclidean distance but not HE?

questions.title: How is an orthogonal matrix learned efficiently during finetuning?
questions.question_body: Equation (5) mentions using Cayley paramterization $R = (I+Q)(I-Q)^{-1}$ with $Q$ skew-symmetric. In practice, how is the inverse computed in a memory‑and‑speed efficient way? Since $R$ must stay orthogonal, do we need to re‑orthogonalise every step? The paper also talks about block‑diagonal matrices; what is the trade‑off between block size $r$ and model flexibility?

questions.title: What exactly is the role of the $ oldsymbol{D}$ scaling matrix in re‑scaled OFT?
questions.question_body: In section 3.4 a diagonal matrix $D$ is introduced to *scale* neuron magnitudes after applying an orthogonal transform. Since hyperspherical energy depends only on directions, reshaping magnitudes should not affect energy. Empirically, does re‑scaled OFT improve convergence or diversity? Is there any risk of exploding norms or numerical instability when learning both $R$ and $D$ simultaneously?

Could you explain why this approximation is valid and how it translates into a practical projection onto the feasible set for $Q$? Also, why does setting a smaller $ eta$ guarantee better stability but may hurt controllability?

questions.title: Why does OFT converge faster than LoRA or vanilla finetuning?
questions.question_body: "It can be viewed as finetuning neurons on a smooth hypersphere manifold" – could you unpack this statement mathematically? How does restricting updates to an orthogonal group reduce the curvature or improve gradient flow compared with unconstrained low‑rank updates? Are there any benchmark experiments that isolate this effect (e.g., training only on a single fully connected layer)?

questions.title: "OFT is agnostic to different architectures" – can I apply it to Transformer attention heads directly?
questions.question_body: The paper says we apply OFT only to attention weights for fair comparison with LoRA. In practice, could I apply OFT to all weight matrices in a Transformer (feed‑forward, embeddings, etc.) without fine‑tun­ing additional hyper‑parameters? Would block‑diagonal structures still be meaningful for sub‑modules like self‑attention multi‑head projections?

questions.title: How does OFT preserve pretraining knowledge while providing strong control signals?
questions.question_body: When training on subject‑driven tasks, control signals are hard; yet OFT seems to keep both semantic consistency and prompt fidelity high. Is this because the orthogonal transform allows re‑orientation of neurons without changing relative geometry? How would you justify that a rotation of neurons suffices to encode new subject information while retaining prior proficiency?

questions.title: "Why not minimize hyperspherical energy" – could minimizing HE hurt control even more?
questions.question_body: "A minimum HE means all neurons are uniformly spaced"—but why would enforcing uniformity destroy pretraining knowledge in diffusion models? Would there be practical experiments where training from scratch with minimum HE leads to better or worse downstream task performance than using pretrained models?

questions.title: "Block‑diagonal parameterization reduces bias" – is there risk of overconstraining certain channels?
questions.question_body: When sharing blocks across channels or using many small blocks, some neuron groups may become correlated; how sensitive is performance to the choice of number of blocks $r$? Does a very small $r$ lead to underfitting, while large $r$ reintroduces risk of collapse similar to full OFT?

questions.title: "No additional inference overhead" – how exactly do we implement inference with learned R?
questions.question_body: "We can simply multiply R by pretrained weight W0 and obtain an equivalent weight W = R W0". In practice, would this multiplication be done at every inference call or once per layer during model preparation? Does it influence memory consumption if R is large but stored as block tables?
